edges/15.description: CALFAN neurologic involvement can include delayed gross motor development.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic mutations in SCYL1 were recently identified as causing a syndromal disorder characterized by peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar atrophy, ataxia, and recurrent episodes of liver failure.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SCYL1 as the causal gene with biallelic mutations producing the core neurohepatic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: A whole-exome sequencing (WES) test revealed that the patient has previously unreported autosomal recessive pathogenic non-sense variation c.895A>T (p.Lys299Ter) in exon 7 of the SCYL1 gene in a homozygous status.
evidence.explanation: Documents a homozygous nonsense (loss-of-function) SCYL1 variant causing the disorder, supporting the loss-of-function mechanism.

genes/0.notes: SCYL1 (SCY1-like pseudokinase 1) on chromosome 11q13.1 encodes an N-terminal kinase-like protein that functions in COPI-mediated retrograde Golgi-to-ER vesicular trafficking. Reported pathogenic variants are predominantly truncating (nonsense/frameshift), consistent with a loss-of-function mechanism. Many reported cases occur in consanguineous families (homozygous), though compound heterozygosity also occurs.

evidence.snippet: Liver crises were triggered by febrile infections and were transient, but fibrosis developed.
evidence.explanation: Transient nature of crises supports a supportive-care management approach during febrile-triggered episodes.

treatments/0.description: Supportive, trigger-focused management of febrile-precipitated cholestatic and acute liver failure crises, including infection control, correction of coagulopathy, nutritional optimization with fat-soluble vitamins, and close monitoring of synthetic liver function. There is no established disease-modifying therapy; crises typically recover with supportive care.

evidence.snippet: To date, three of 18 patients reported underwent liver transplantation in infancy and early childhood (7-23 months).
evidence.explanation: Documents liver transplantation as a management option in CALFAN syndrome.

evidence.snippet: At the most recent follow-up, 3 years after transplantation, the patient is doing well.
evidence.explanation: Reports favorable hepatic outcome 3 years after liver transplantation in early adulthood.

treatments/1.description: Liver transplantation for progressive or recurrent liver failure not controlled by supportive care. Reported in infancy/early childhood and, in one case, in early adulthood with favorable 3-year graft outcome. Transplantation addresses hepatic disease but does not arrest neurodegeneration, which may persist.

evidence.snippet: Physical therapy improved quality of life, functional independence, trunk control, and upper extremity performance.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates functional benefit of physical therapy in CALFAN syndrome.

treatments/2.description: Individualized physical therapy program (trunk stabilization, balance training, functional exercises) improving quality of life, functional independence, trunk control, and upper-extremity performance in a child with CALFAN syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Seven patients from five families with biallelic SCYL1 variants were identified.
evidence.explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance with biallelic variants underpins the need for recurrence-risk genetic counseling.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence-risk counseling, cascade testing, and reproductive options for at-risk families, including prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing.

evidence.snippet: All of the missense mutations found in AFF4 (c.760A>G (p.Thr254Ala), c.761C>G (p.Thr254Ser) and c.772C>T (p.Arg258Trp)) were de novo
evidence.explanation: Reports the three founding alleles and their de novo status.

evidence.snippet: All 3 missense mutations were located within the ALF (AF4/LAF4/FMR2) homology domain of AFF4, and these missense mutations altered highly evolutionarily conserved amino acids
evidence.explanation: Localises the lesion to the ALF homology domain and notes the conservation of the affected residues.

evidence.snippet: All the mutations identified in CHOPS syndrome were de novo, and those clustered in the ALF homology domain
evidence.explanation: Confirms clustering and de novo origin across an eleven-individual cohort.

evidence.snippet: The p. R258W mutation represents the most common recurrent mutation, and this mutation accounted for 55% of CHOPS syndrome cases.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the recurrent allele and its share of reported cases.

evidence.snippet: there are no missense variants reported in this region in ExAC
evidence.explanation: Population-database constraint on the affected 14-amino-acid stretch, which is why variants there are interpretable as pathogenic.

evidence.snippet: To date, all CHOPS-related pathogenic variants are located in the AFF4 ALF homology domain.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews restates the domain restriction as a diagnostic rule.

steps/1.description: A single heterozygous de novo missense variant in AFF4 (chromosome 5q31.1). The reported alleles cluster in a 14-amino-acid stretch (residues ~251-263) of the ALF (AF4/LAF4/FMR2) homology domain: p.Pro253Arg, p.Pro253Leu, p.Thr254Ala, p.Thr254Ser, p.Ala255Thr, p.Ala255Val, p.Arg258Trp, p.Met260Thr and p.Met260Val. p.Arg258Trp is the recurrent allele. This node records the genomic lesion only; no truncating or whole-gene-deletion allele has been implicated, which is itself an argument against haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: the AFF4 constructs containing the missense mutations found in the three CHOPS syndrome probands hindered the degradation of AFF4 with SIAH1 overexpression
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that the CHOPS alleles escape SIAH1-mediated degradation.

evidence.snippet: The addition of MG132, which is a proteosomal degradation inhibitor, resulted in the recovery of AFF4 bands.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the proteasome as the degradation route being escaped.

evidence.snippet: both p.A255T and p.P253R mutants showed a similar resistance to degradation when co-transfected with SIAH1 as the p.T254A mutant
evidence.explanation: Extends the same degradation-resistance mechanism to two later-identified alleles.

steps/2.description: Wild-type AFF4 is cleared by the SIAH1 ubiquitin E3 ligase through the proteasome. Co-expression experiments in HEK293T cells show that each CHOPS allele resists SIAH1-driven degradation, and proteasome inhibition with MG132 restores wild-type AFF4 levels - confirming the route being escaped is proteasomal. The same escape was demonstrated independently for the later alleles p.Ala255Thr and p.Pro253Arg. This is a protein-turnover defect, distinct from the abundance change it produces.

evidence.snippet: The amount of AFF4 protein in patient derived skin fibroblasts was elevated, supporting the suggestion that the missense mutations found in these probands results in a more stable AFF4 protein
evidence.explanation: Establishes AFF4 protein accumulation in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: accumulation of AFF4 mainly occurred on the chromatin fraction in the CHOPS syndrome cell lines
evidence.explanation: Localises the excess AFF4 to chromatin, which is where it acts.

evidence.snippet: The amount of other SEC components such as ELL2 and CDK9 did not show major alterations in the chromatin fraction of the CHOPS syndrome cell lines.
evidence.explanation: Shows the accumulation is scaffold-specific rather than a uniform increase in the whole complex - the reason this node is worth separating from SEC activity.

steps/3.description: AFF4 protein is elevated in patient-derived skin fibroblasts while AFF4 mRNA is unchanged, confirming a post-translational cause. The excess partitions specifically to the chromatin fraction, and the other SEC components ELL2 and CDK9 are not correspondingly increased - so the complex is not simply more abundant; its scaffold is over-represented on chromatin. Deleting the mutant allele in a patient line lowers AFF4 back down, attributing the accumulation to the mutant allele rather than to a trans effect.

evidence.snippet: Transcriptional elongation is critical for gene expression regulation during embryogenesis. The super elongation complex (SEC) governs this process by mobilizing paused RNA polymerase II (RNAP2).
evidence.explanation: States the normal function of the complex whose activity is dysregulated here.

evidence.snippet: CDK9 phosphorylates the Ser2 residue of RNAP2 in order for initiation of transcriptional elongation
evidence.explanation: Names the molecular step by which the SEC licenses productive elongation.

evidence.snippet: The up-regulation of 5 of these genes was statistically significant: MYC, JUN, TMEM100, ZNF711 and FAM13C. These observations further support the notion that AFF4 mutations render gain-of-function effects.
evidence.explanation: Quantitative evidence that direct AFF4 targets are de-repressed, and the authors' own basis for calling the mechanism gain of function.

evidence.snippet: Transcriptome and chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) analyses demonstrated similar alterations of genome-wide binding of AFF4, cohesin and RNAP2 in CdLS and CHOPS syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Genome-wide evidence that AFF4, cohesin and RNAP2 deployment is altered.

evidence.snippet: AFF1 mainly binds upstream of the TSS, while AFF4 is enriched downstream of the TSS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that AFF4 specifically occupies the post-initiation region where elongation is controlled, which is why an excess of chromatin-bound AFF4 is expected to act on elongation rather than on initiation. This is general cell biology in non-CHOPS cells, not a patient-derived observation.

evidence.snippet: disruption of AFF4 results in slow elongation and early termination in a subset of AFF4-bound active genes, whereas AFF1 deletion leads to fast elongation and transcriptional readthrough in the same subset of genes
evidence.explanation: Shows AFF4 dosage on chromatin sets elongation rate and termination in a gene-selective way. Graded INDIRECT because the experiment is AFF4 loss, the opposite direction from the CHOPS gain of function, so the claim follows by an inference step rather than being asserted by the quoted result.

steps/4.description: The super elongation complex mobilises promoter-proximally paused RNA polymerase II, with its P-TEFb (CDK9-cyclin T1) module phosphorylating Ser2 of the RNAP2 C-terminal domain to license productive elongation. With AFF4 over-represented on chromatin, genome-wide binding of AFF4, RNAP2 and cohesin is altered and direct AFF4 target genes are de-repressed: MYC, JUN, TMEM100, ZNF711 and FAM13C are all significantly upregulated in patient fibroblasts. This is the gain-of-function read-out that names the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: In both patient cells, we found a decrease in cohesin, NIPBL, BRD4, and acetylation of lysine 27 on histone H3
evidence.explanation: Reports the loss of enhancer-complex components in CHOPS patient cells.

evidence.snippet: By contrast, TADs were maintained in both patient cells.
evidence.explanation: Bounds the claim: the defect is enhancer/loop-level, not TAD-level.

evidence.snippet: These findings reveal a shared molecular mechanism in these syndromes and highlight unexpected roles for cohesin, cohesin loaders, and the SEC in maintaining the enhancer complexes.
evidence.explanation: States the shared-mechanism conclusion linking CHOPS syndrome to CdLS.

steps/5.description: Chromosome-architecture analysis of CHOPS and CdLS patient cell lines found cohesin, the cohesin loader NIPBL, BRD4 and H3K27ac all reduced at most enhancers, with attenuation of enhancer-promoter loops, while topologically associating domains were preserved. The lesion is therefore at the level of enhancer complex maintenance and looping, not at the level of large-scale genome compartmentalisation - and it is shared with CdLS, which is the structural basis of the two disorders' phenotypic overlap.

evidence.snippet: upregulated genes are enriched for Homeobox proteins, skeletal system development/morphogenesis and anterior/posterior pattern formation as well as embryonic organ development/morphogenesis, and downregulated genes are enriched for actin binding genes and extracellular matrix genes
evidence.explanation: Characterises which developmental programmes are disturbed, connecting the molecular lesion to a skeletal and organ-morphogenesis phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Some genetic disorders caused by mutations in genes encoding components of the transcriptional machinery as well as proteins involved in epigenetic modification of the genome share many overlapping features, such as facial dysmorphisms, growth problems and developmental delay/intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Places CHOPS syndrome in the disorders-of-transcriptional-regulation class and explains why global transcriptional disturbance yields this phenotype triad.

steps/6.description: Expression profiling of patient fibroblasts identifies hundreds of dysregulated genes. Upregulated genes are enriched for homeobox proteins, skeletal system development and morphogenesis, anterior/posterior pattern formation, and embryonic organ development; downregulated genes are enriched for actin-binding and extracellular-matrix genes. The dysregulated set correlates positively with that of CdLS fibroblasts. This is the disorder-agnostic convergence point that CHOPS syndrome shares with the wider class of transcriptional-regulation disorders.

evidence.snippet: Excessive food-seeking behaviors and over-affection were common in all individuals, in addition to pulmonary involvement, which are not seen in CdLS
evidence.explanation: Establishes food-seeking behaviour as a consistent and CHOPS-discriminating feature.

evidence.snippet: The group of questions pertaining to impairment of satiety category had the highest average scores ranging from 3 to 4.5.
evidence.explanation: Instrumented evidence that satiety, specifically, is impaired.

evidence.snippet: Neurobehavioral features include disruptive and self-absorbed behaviors, communication disturbance, and food-seeking behaviors leading to obesity.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews places food-seeking behaviour causally upstream of the obesity.

steps/7.description: Excessive food-seeking behaviour with impaired satiety is near-universal and is one of the features that distinguishes CHOPS syndrome from CdLS. On a food-related problems questionnaire originally designed for Prader-Willi syndrome, the impairment-of-satiety items scored highest, every respondent reported their child helping themselves to forbidden food, and most families had found it necessary to lock food away. The node is behavioural and deliberately makes no hypothalamic claim - no mechanism linking AFF4 to appetite regulation has been demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: These individuals have a distinct phenotype, that is, characterized by short stature, characteristic facial features (synophrys, arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, upturned nasal tip with anteverted nares and coarse, full facies), congenital heart defects, pulmonary involvement, brachydactyly and other skeletal involvement, genitourinary issues, and developmental delay/intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the organ systems that converge at this node.

evidence.snippet: The patient exhibited significant growth failure despite an adequate growth hormone response.
evidence.explanation: Shows the growth failure is not attributable to growth hormone deficiency, which is why it is placed at the developmental-programme node rather than at a pituitary one.

steps/8.description: The organism-level convergence node: craniofacial, cardiac, pulmonary, skeletal, genitourinary, ocular and neurodevelopmental structures are all affected, with linear growth failure that is not corrected by a normal growth hormone response. Phenotypes attach here.

evidence.snippet: All individuals reported to date have mild-to-moderate developmental delay and intellectual disability without regression.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states both the universality and the mild-to-moderate severity, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: All individuals with CHOPS syndrome had developmental delay, and varying degrees of intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort confirmation that the feature is universal.

steps/9.description: Every individual reported has developmental delay with mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, and importantly without regression. Motor milestones are substantially delayed - independent walking at an average of 4.8 years in the eleven-individual cohort.

evidence.snippet: The age at which individuals with CHOPS syndrome started rolling ranges between 9 and 15 months (average: 12 months), age to sit independently ranges between 11 months and 3 years (average: 18 months), and age to walk independently ranges between 3 and 6 years (average: 4.8 years).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the delay across motor milestones.

steps/10.description: Delay across motor and communication domains from infancy; rolling at an average of 12 months, sitting at 18 months, and independent walking between 3 and 6 years.

evidence.snippet: Excessive food-seeking behaviors and over-affection were common in all individuals, in addition to pulmonary involvement, which are not seen in CdLS
evidence.explanation: Reports the behaviour in all individuals of the cohort, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: food-seeking behaviors leading to obesity
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews independently records the behaviour and its consequence.

steps/11.description: Preoccupation with food and impaired satiety, requiring food to be locked away in most families. This is the behavioural driver of the obesity and one of the features distinguishing CHOPS syndrome from Cornelia de Lange syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Neurobehavioral features include disruptive and self-absorbed behaviors, communication disturbance, and food-seeking behaviors leading to obesity.
evidence.explanation: Names the behavioural domains affected.

evidence.snippet: Most problematic behaviors in all individuals included disruptive, self-absorbed, and communication disturbance behaviors.
evidence.explanation: Instrumented behavioural assessment identifying the same domains.

steps/12.description: Behavioural profile on the Developmental Behaviour Checklist is dominated by disruptive, self-absorbed and communication-disturbance behaviours, including temper tantrums and disrobing. Notably, significant autistic behaviour was not observed in the reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: Common disruptive behaviors included excessive food seeking behaviors, throwing off clothes, and temper tantrums.
evidence.explanation: Names temper tantrums as a recurrent behaviour. No denominator is given, so no frequency band is asserted.

steps/13.description: Temper tantrums are named among the recurrent disruptive behaviours, alongside food-seeking and disrobing.

evidence.snippet: Excessive food-seeking behaviors and over-affection were common in all individuals, in addition to pulmonary involvement, which are not seen in CdLS
evidence.explanation: Reports over-affection in all individuals of the cohort, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band, and marks it as a CHOPS-discriminating feature.

steps/14.description: Indiscriminate over-affection was reported in all individuals of the cohort and, like the food-seeking behaviour, is one of the features not seen in Cornelia de Lange syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Coarse facies and round face with full cheeks become more noticeable with age.
evidence.explanation: Records both the feature and its progressive character.

evidence.snippet: Additional distinctive facial dysmorphia included anteverted nares, coarse facies, and facial fullness
evidence.explanation: Cohort confirmation of coarse facies and facial fullness.

steps/15.description: Coarse facies with a round face and full cheeks, becoming progressively more recognisable with age. This evolution is one of the features that eventually separates the CHOPS gestalt from the CdLS gestalt, which the younger face resembles.

evidence.snippet: All 11 individuals presented with features reminiscent of Cornelia de Lange syndrome such as synophrys, upturned nasal tip, arched eyebrows, and long eyelashes.
evidence.explanation: Reports synophrys in 11 of 11 individuals, supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

steps/16.description: Confluent eyebrows, present in all eleven individuals of the reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: All 11 individuals presented with features reminiscent of Cornelia de Lange syndrome such as synophrys, upturned nasal tip, arched eyebrows, and long eyelashes.
evidence.explanation: Arched eyebrows reported in 11 of 11 individuals.

steps/17.description: Arched, thick eyebrows, part of the CdLS-like facial gestalt.

evidence.snippet: All 11 individuals presented with features reminiscent of Cornelia de Lange syndrome such as synophrys, upturned nasal tip, arched eyebrows, and long eyelashes.
evidence.explanation: Long eyelashes reported in 11 of 11 individuals.

steps/18.description: Trichomegaly of the eyelashes, a shared feature with CdLS.

evidence.snippet: Characteristic facial features include synophrys, highly arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, proptosis, and anteverted nares.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists anteverted nares among the characteristic facial features.

steps/19.description: Upturned nasal tip with anteverted nares.

evidence.snippet: Characteristic facial features include synophrys, highly arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, proptosis, and anteverted nares.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists proptosis among the characteristic facial features.

steps/20.description: Prominent, protruding globes contributing to the facial gestalt.

evidence.snippet: Other noted recurrent features were large anterior fontanelle (Case-1, 2, 5), and Wormian skull bones (Case-1, 5).
evidence.explanation: Names the three individuals with a large anterior fontanelle; three of eleven is 27%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/21.description: A large anterior fontanelle was a recurrent finding in three of the eleven individuals of the cohort.

evidence.snippet: Extraoral examination revealed midface hypoplasia, thick eyebrows, broad forehead, large ears, and coarse facial appearance.
evidence.explanation: Single detailed dentofacial case description; frequency is deliberately omitted because this rests on one report.

steps/22.description: Midface hypoplasia noted on extraoral examination in a detailed dentofacial assessment, alongside a broad forehead and large ears.

evidence.snippet: All 11 individuals had short stature and obesity.
evidence.explanation: 11 of 11 individuals, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: However, the measurements at the latest clinic visit indicated average height was around −5 SD, although HC remained around −2 SD
evidence.explanation: Documents the progressive worsening of the height deficit.

evidence.snippet: The patient exhibited significant growth failure despite an adequate growth hormone response.
evidence.explanation: Shows growth failure is not explained by growth hormone deficiency.

steps/23.description: Short stature is universal and progressive: birth length averages -2 to -3 SD but height at latest follow-up averages around -5 SD, while head circumference stays near -2 SD. Growth failure persists despite an adequate growth hormone response.

evidence.snippet: All 11 individuals had short stature and obesity.
evidence.explanation: 11 of 11 individuals, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Obesity, pulmonary involvement, skeletal findings, and distinct craniofacial features are the most notable features distinguishing CHOPS syndrome from CdLS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes obesity as a discriminating feature against the main differential.

steps/24.description: Obesity with weight percentiles disproportionately higher than height percentiles. Together with pulmonary involvement and skeletal findings, obesity is one of the features most reliably distinguishing CHOPS syndrome from CdLS, where growth restriction affects weight as well as height.

evidence.snippet: Congenital heart disease was present in 8 of the 11 individuals reported here. Of these eight individuals, six had a patent ductus arteriosis (PDA)
evidence.explanation: Six of eleven individuals is 55%, within the FREQUENT band.

steps/25.description: The most common congenital heart defect in CHOPS syndrome, present in six of the eight individuals with congenital heart disease in the eleven-individual cohort.

evidence.snippet: five had a ventricular septal defect (VSD)
evidence.explanation: Five of eleven individuals is 45%, within the FREQUENT band.

steps/26.description: The second most common cardiac lesion, in five of the eleven individuals of the reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: and three had a patent foramen ovale (PFO)
evidence.explanation: Three of eleven individuals is 27%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/27.description: Present in three of the eleven individuals of the reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: three subjects (Case-2, 3, 9) required a tracheostomy, with two of these having laryngomalacia (Case-2, 3).
evidence.explanation: Two of eleven individuals is 18%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Additional features included congenital cataracts, laryngomalacia, and mild mitral insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Independent case report of laryngomalacia in CHOPS syndrome.

steps/28.description: Upper-airway collapse contributing to the respiratory burden; two of the three tracheostomised individuals in the cohort had laryngomalacia, and it is also described in an independent case report.

evidence.snippet: Structurally, two cases (Case-2, 6, 7) had subglottic stenosis, and Case-3 had a congenital narrow oropharynx.
evidence.explanation: Structural airway narrowing in the cohort. Note the source's own case list is internally inconsistent (it says "two cases" but names three); the OCCASIONAL band covers either reading.

steps/29.description: Fixed structural narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords, distinct from the dynamic collapse of laryngomalacia and a separate reason for tracheostomy.

evidence.snippet: Brachydactyly was present in 8 out of the 11 individuals.
evidence.explanation: Eight of eleven individuals is 73%, within the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Other common features include growth deficiency, respiratory issues, congenital heart defects, small hands, brachydactyly, ocular abnormalities, genitourinary abnormalities, and gastrointestinal manifestations.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews independently lists small hands and brachydactyly as common.

steps/30.description: Short digits with small hands, present in eight of eleven individuals; the most consistent skeletal finding.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal abnormalities are also common, and those include abnormal shape of vertebral bodies, hypoplastic long bones, and low bone mineral density.
evidence.explanation: Reports abnormal vertebral body shape as a common skeletal finding.

evidence.snippet: An abnormal shape of the vertebral bodies with decreased height, pronounced from T8 to L1, was noted in Case-1
evidence.explanation: Radiographic detail of the vertebral involvement.

steps/31.description: Vertebral bodies of abnormal shape with decreased height, anterior beaking, congenital vertebral fusion and narrowed intervertebral disc spaces are reported across the cohort - the "skeletal dysplasia" of the acronym.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal abnormalities are also common, and those include abnormal shape of vertebral bodies, hypoplastic long bones, and low bone mineral density.
evidence.explanation: Names low bone mineral density among the common skeletal features.

evidence.snippet: Panoramic radiography demonstrated reduced bone mineralization and agenesis of all second premolars and Tooth 47.
evidence.explanation: Independent radiographic observation of reduced mineralisation in the jaws.

steps/32.description: Low bone mineral density is reported as a common skeletal finding, and reduced bone mineralisation was independently noted on panoramic radiography in a dentofacial case study.

evidence.snippet: Other noted recurrent features were large anterior fontanelle (Case-1, 2, 5), and Wormian skull bones (Case-1, 5).
evidence.explanation: Names the two individuals with Wormian skull bones; two of eleven is 18%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/33.description: Accessory sutural bones in the cranial sutures, reported in two of the eleven individuals. Wormian bones and the wide anterior fontanel together indicate delayed or abnormal cranial ossification, consistent with the reduced bone mineral density recorded separately.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal abnormalities are also common, and those include abnormal shape of vertebral bodies, hypoplastic long bones, and low bone mineral density.
evidence.explanation: Lists hypoplastic long bones among the common skeletal features. The sentence gives no denominator, which is why frequency is omitted.

evidence.snippet: Hypoplasia of the proximal radii bilaterally, hypoplasia of the fibula bilaterally was noted in Case-3
evidence.explanation: Radiographic detail naming the specific long bones affected.

steps/34.description: Long-bone hypoplasia is listed among the common skeletal findings, with bilateral hypoplasia of the proximal radii and of the fibulae documented radiographically in one individual, and shortening of the proximal humeri and metacarpals with hypoplastic distal phalanges in another. No frequency is asserted because the summary sentence gives no count. The binding shifts the claim from hypoplasia to shortness: every synonym on HP:0003026 is about shortening, and HPO has no long-bone-level hypoplasia term. It is accepted here because the same paper's radiographic detail documents shortening of the proximal humeri and metacarpals, and because the previous HP:0045060 binding was broader still - whole extremity, and covering aplasia as well as hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Other common features include growth deficiency, respiratory issues, congenital heart defects, small hands, brachydactyly, ocular abnormalities, genitourinary abnormalities, and gastrointestinal manifestations.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists small hands among the common features.

evidence.snippet: Other reported abnormalities included myopia (Case-2, 8, 9), strabismus (Case-5, 8), cataracts (Case-3, 9, 10), ptosis (Case-5, 6), hypothyroidism (Case-4), acanthosis nigricans and skin changes (Case-5, 8), and gynecomastia (Case-5).
evidence.explanation: Three of eleven individuals is 27%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Additional features included congenital cataracts, laryngomalacia, and mild mitral insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Independent report of congenital cataract.

steps/36.description: Cataracts, including congenital cataracts, in three of the eleven individuals of the cohort and in an independent case report; GeneReviews recommends subspecialist treatment.

evidence.snippet: Other reported abnormalities included myopia (Case-2, 8, 9), strabismus (Case-5, 8), cataracts (Case-3, 9, 10), ptosis (Case-5, 6), hypothyroidism (Case-4), acanthosis nigricans and skin changes (Case-5, 8), and gynecomastia (Case-5).
evidence.explanation: Three of eleven individuals is 27%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Assess for myopia and strabismus per ophthalmologist and at least annually; annual audiology evaluation.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews treats myopia as expected enough to warrant annual surveillance.

steps/37.description: Refractive error in three of eleven individuals; GeneReviews makes annual ophthalmological assessment for myopia and strabismus a surveillance recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Other reported abnormalities included myopia (Case-2, 8, 9), strabismus (Case-5, 8), cataracts (Case-3, 9, 10), ptosis (Case-5, 6), hypothyroidism (Case-4), acanthosis nigricans and skin changes (Case-5, 8), and gynecomastia (Case-5).
evidence.explanation: Two of eleven individuals is 18%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/38.description: Ocular misalignment, reported in two of eleven individuals.

evidence.snippet: Other reported abnormalities included myopia (Case-2, 8, 9), strabismus (Case-5, 8), cataracts (Case-3, 9, 10), ptosis (Case-5, 6), hypothyroidism (Case-4), acanthosis nigricans and skin changes (Case-5, 8), and gynecomastia (Case-5).
evidence.explanation: Two of eleven individuals is 18%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/39.description: Drooping eyelids, reported in two of eleven individuals.

evidence.snippet: Eight out of 11 individuals were reported to have some type of hearing loss
evidence.explanation: Eight of eleven individuals is 73%, within the FREQUENT band.

steps/40.description: Some form of hearing loss in eight of eleven individuals; annual audiology evaluation is a GeneReviews surveillance recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Six individuals (Case-2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10) required G-tube insertion.
evidence.explanation: Six of eleven individuals is 55%, within the FREQUENT band.

steps/41.description: Six of the eleven individuals required gastrostomy tube placement, and feeding therapy plus G-tube placement as needed is a GeneReviews management recommendation. Note this coexists with hyperphagia later in life - the feeding problem is one of safe oral intake, not of appetite.

evidence.snippet: Genital abnormalities in males included cryptorchidism (Case-2), hypospadias (Case-5), and small genitalia (Case-5 and Case-11).
evidence.explanation: Single-individual observation; frequency omitted since the denominator is males only and the count is one.

steps/42.description: Undescended testes, reported in a male in the cohort.

evidence.snippet: Genital abnormalities in males included cryptorchidism (Case-2), hypospadias (Case-5), and small genitalia (Case-5 and Case-11).
evidence.explanation: Single-individual observation; frequency omitted for the same reason.

steps/43.description: Reported in a male in the cohort, alongside small genitalia.

evidence.snippet: Genital abnormalities in males included cryptorchidism (Case-2), hypospadias (Case-5), and small genitalia (Case-5 and Case-11).
evidence.explanation: Names the two individuals with small genitalia. Frequency is omitted because the denominator is males only and is not stated.

steps/44.description: Hypoplastic external genitalia in two of the male individuals in the cohort, reported in the same sentence as the cryptorchidism and hypospadias. No genital abnormality was reported in any female.

evidence.snippet: Other anomalies of the genitourinary system included horseshoe kidney (Case-1, 5) and vesicoureteral reflux (Case-2, 3).
evidence.explanation: Two of eleven individuals is 18%, within the OCCASIONAL band.

genes/0.notes: AFF4 (chromosome 5q31.1) encodes the scaffold subunit of the super elongation complex. Every CHOPS allele is a missense change within a highly conserved 14-amino-acid stretch of the ALF homology domain (approximately residues 251-263), which carries the SIAH1 degron. p.Arg258Trp is recurrent and accounted for 55% of cases in the largest published series; p.Pro253Arg, p.Pro253Leu, p.Thr254Ala, p.Thr254Ser, p.Ala255Thr, p.Ala255Val, p.Met260Thr and p.Met260Val are also reported. The mechanism is gain of function through escape from proteasomal degradation, not haploinsufficiency - no truncating allele has been implicated, and the restriction of pathogenic variation to this one small domain is what makes targeted AFF4 sequencing a viable diagnostic route.

open_questions/0.rationale: Pulmonary involvement is one of the two features that most reliably separate CHOPS syndrome from CdLS, and it carries much of the morbidity - a third of the largest cohort required tracheostomy. Yet the largest clinical series states plainly that the aetiology of the chronic lung disease is undetermined, and it is not attributed to the cardiac lesions, prematurity, or aspiration. Nothing in the published transcriptomic work identifies a lung-specific programme downstream of excess AFF4. The structural airway anomalies (laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis) are wired into the pathograph as congenital malformations, but the parenchymal and functional pulmonary phenotypes named above are deliberately left without a causal edge rather than inventing a pulmonary mechanism.

open_questions/1.rationale: The obesity of CHOPS syndrome is behaviourally driven: satiety items score highest on a Prader-Willi-derived questionnaire, and families lock food away. But no hypothalamic, leptin-melanocortin, or other appetite-pathway link to AFF4 has been demonstrated, and the phenotypic resemblance to Prader-Willi syndrome is not evidence of a shared mechanism. The causal edge into this node is therefore curated as INDIRECT and the node makes no anatomical claim.

open_questions/2.rationale: One individual with a p.Pro253Leu AFF4 variant developed moyamoya disease and diffuse narrowing of the renal arteries and infrarenal aorta. The observation is confounded: the same individual carried the RNF213 p.Arg4810Lys moyamoya susceptibility allele inherited from an unaffected mother. With n=1 and a competing explanation in the same genome, this cannot be curated as a CHOPS feature; the report's own authors ask for more observation. The phenotype is therefore recorded with the confounder carried as its own REFUTE item and the authors' hedge as NO_EVIDENCE, so that a second case would be recognised as confirmatory rather than novel.

open_questions/3.rationale: CHOPS and CdLS patient cells converge on the same enhancer and looping defect, which plausibly accounts for the shared features - synophrys, arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, developmental delay, heart defects, hearing loss. But obesity, pulmonary involvement and skeletal dysplasia are CHOPS-specific and would have to arise from something the shared mechanism does not explain, presumably the elongation-side gain of function. No study has yet partitioned the phenotype between the two arms, so the pathograph runs both into a single convergence node rather than assigning phenotypes to one arm or the other.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy; supportive management of encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and metabolic decompensation.

evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing identified biallelic missense variants in COX6A2, which is expressed only in the skeletal muscle and heart.
evidence.explanation: Establishes COX6A2 as a striated-muscle-restricted Complex IV subunit, the protein affected in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: Assembly of complex IV and its supercomplex formation were impaired in the muscle.
evidence.explanation: Impaired Complex IV assembly and supercomplex formation in patient muscle demonstrates failed holoenzyme biogenesis.

steps/1.description: Biallelic COX6A2 missense variants disrupt the heart/skeletal-muscle isoform of the nuclear-encoded structural subunit VIa of Complex IV. Because COX6A2 is expressed only in striated muscle, the consequence is a tissue-restricted failure of Complex IV biogenesis: assembly of the holoenzyme and its incorporation into respiratory supercomplexes is impaired in muscle, while other organs are spared.

evidence.snippet: We found specific reductions in complex IV activities in the skeletal muscle of both individuals.
evidence.explanation: Reduced Complex IV enzymatic activity in patient skeletal muscle establishes the functional terminal-electron-transfer deficit.

steps/2.description: Reduced amounts and activity of assembled Complex IV block electron transfer from cytochrome c to oxygen and proton pumping, impairing oxidative ATP synthesis in striated muscle. In both COX6A2-deficient individuals, Complex IV activity was specifically reduced in skeletal muscle.

evidence.snippet: Both patients presented muscle weakness and hypotonia in 4 limbs along with facial muscle weakness.
evidence.explanation: Skeletal muscle weakness and hypotonia are the dominant high-energy-tissue manifestations of the muscle bioenergetic deficit.

evidence.snippet: One patient had cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: Cardiac muscle, which also expresses COX6A2, can be affected, manifesting as cardiomyopathy.

steps/3.description: The bioenergetic deficit manifests selectively in striated muscle, the only tissue expressing COX6A2. Both reported individuals had limb and facial muscle weakness with hypotonia, and one had cardiomyopathy, with no involvement of other organs — distinguishing this entity from the encephalopathic and multisystem presentations of other nuclear COX deficiencies.

evidence.snippet: Both patients presented muscle weakness and hypotonia in 4 limbs along with facial muscle weakness.
evidence.explanation: Both reported individuals had muscle weakness affecting the limbs and face.

steps/4.description: Limb and facial muscle weakness in all reported COX6A2-deficient individuals, reflecting the striated-muscle-specific Complex IV deficiency.

evidence.snippet: One patient had cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: One of the two reported individuals had cardiomyopathy.

steps/5.description: Cardiomyopathy in one of the two reported individuals, reflecting involvement of cardiac striated muscle, which also expresses COX6A2.

edges/1.description: Failure to assemble Complex IV yields a catalytically deficient holoenzyme in muscle.

edges/2.description: The muscle bioenergetic deficit injures high-demand striated muscle, producing myopathy and cardiomyopathy.

edges/3.description: Striated muscle energy failure manifests as limb and facial muscle weakness.

edges/4.description: Cardiac muscle involvement manifests as cardiomyopathy in a subset of patients.

evidence.snippet: This study indicates that biallelic variants in COX6A2 cause a striated muscle-specific form of COX deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Identifies biallelic COX6A2 variants as the cause of a striated-muscle-specific Complex IV deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing identified biallelic missense variants in COX6A2, which is expressed only in the skeletal muscle and heart.
evidence.explanation: Whole exome sequencing identified the causal biallelic COX6A2 variants.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists; management is supportive, addressing the muscle weakness, hypotonia, and cardiomyopathy with multidisciplinary supportive care.

evidence.snippet: Structural analysis indicated that the Arg87 residue is buried at an interface between CYFIP2 and WAVE1, and the Arg87 variant may disrupt hydrogen bonding, leading to structural instability and aberrant activation of the WAVE regulatory complex
evidence.explanation: Locates the hotspot residue structurally and states the predicted consequence for the complex.

evidence.snippet: Asp724 as second mutational hotspot (4/19 cases)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second hotspot and its frequency in the expanded cohort.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion. Variants cluster at two hotspots, p.Arg87 and p.Asp724. Arg87 is buried at the interface between CYFIP2 and WAVE1 inside the assembled complex, which is why substituting it destabilises the interface rather than simply removing a surface contact. Variants scattered elsewhere in the primary sequence converge on the same interface in three dimensions.

evidence.snippet: All mutant CYFIP2 showed comparatively weaker interactions to the VCA domain than wild-type CYFIP2
evidence.explanation: The direct binding measurement, reported for every mutant tested.

steps/2.description: Mutant CYFIP2 binds the VCA domain more weakly than wild type. Because the complex works by sequestering VCA, weaker binding means less effective autoinhibition. This node is the measured binding change, kept separate from the downstream actin readout.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrated that the p.Arg87Cys variant enhances ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of CYFIP2
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration of the degradation mechanism in the knock-in mouse and cellular models.

evidence.snippet: Beyond identifying a decrease in CYFIP2 protein levels in the Cyfip2+/R87C brains
evidence.explanation: Records the reduced steady-state protein abundance that the degradation mechanism produces, in brain tissue.

steps/3.description: A second consequence of p.Arg87Cys: the variant protein is ubiquitinated and degraded more readily, lowering steady-state CYFIP2 abundance in the brain. This is the observation that sits in tension with a pure gain-of-function reading, and it is curated as its own node rather than folded into the interface account.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that de novo Arg87 variants in CYFIP2 have gain-of-function effects on the WAVE signaling pathway and are associated with severe neurological disorders
evidence.explanation: States the gain-of-function interpretation of the WAVE pathway effect.

steps/4.description: Release of the WAVE VCA domain from autoinhibition, activating the complex outside normal RAC1 control. This is the node the gain-of-function account turns on.

evidence.snippet: Immunofluorescence revealed that ectopic speckled accumulation of actin and CYFIP2 was significantly increased in cells transfected with mutant CYFIP2
evidence.explanation: The original actin readout in a heterologous transfection system.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with its role in WRC-mediated actin polymerization we substantiate aberrant regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in patient fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Confirms the same cellular abnormality in primary cells from affected individuals rather than in an overexpression model.

steps/5.description: The cellular convergence point of both proposed molecular routes. Abnormal actin accumulation was shown first in transfected cells and subsequently substantiated in patient-derived fibroblasts, which matters because it moves the finding out of an overexpression system into primary patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Age-progressive cytoarchitectural disorganization and gliosis were also identified in the hippocampus of Cyfip2+/R87C mice
evidence.explanation: Structural correlate in the hippocampus of the genotype-matched mouse, and records that it worsens with age.

evidence.snippet: This progression was associated with synaptic remodeling, sequential activation of different glial cell types, lipid droplet accumulation in astrocytes, and significant proteomic and lipidomic changes in the brain
evidence.explanation: Establishes synaptic remodeling and staged glial involvement as accompaniments of seizure evolution rather than a static finding.

steps/6.description: In neurons the WAVE complex drives actin remodeling at dendritic spines and growth cones, so dysregulated actin dynamics translate into abnormal synaptic architecture. The knock-in mouse shows age-progressive cytoarchitectural disorganization and gliosis in the hippocampus, and longitudinal work shows the synaptic remodeling is itself time-dependent rather than a fixed lesion.

evidence.snippet: after an initial period of neonatal spasms, Cyfip2+/R87C mice entered a seizure-free phase, followed by spontaneous recurrent seizures in adulthood
evidence.explanation: Establishes that network excitability in this model changes over time in three distinct phases.

steps/7.description: The circuit-level state that produces seizures. In the mouse model this is not a fixed property but evolves through distinct stages, which is what makes the model's temporal structure informative rather than incidental.

evidence.snippet: sequential activation of different glial cell types, lipid droplet accumulation in astrocytes
evidence.explanation: Records the staged glial response and the astrocytic lipid phenotype.

steps/8.description: Sequential activation of different glial populations over the disease course in the mouse model, accompanied by lipid droplet accumulation in astrocytes. Curated as its own node because it is a distinct tissue-level process with its own time course, not a restatement of the synaptic finding.

evidence.snippet: We identified three de novo CYFIP2 variants at the Arg87 residue in 4 unrelated individuals with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Establishes the early-onset epileptic encephalopathy phenotype in the founding cohort.

steps/9.description: Early-onset seizures that characteristically resist antiseizure medication, frequently presenting as epileptic spasms in a West syndrome pattern.

edges/1.description: The structural lesion acts first on the interface it sits in.

edges/2.description: A second, mechanistically separate consequence demonstrated for p.Arg87Cys. Drawn as a parallel edge from the variant rather than downstream of the interface defect, because the two are competing accounts of the same variant rather than sequential steps - see the controversy discussion.

edges/3.description: Loss of VCA sequestration is what releases the complex.

edges/4.description: Reduced CYFIP2 abundance is proposed to reach the same actin readout by a different route than interface destabilization.

edges/5.description: An activated complex nucleates actin.

edges/6.description: Actin dynamics are the substrate for spine and synapse remodeling in neurons.

edges/7.description: Glial activation accompanies the evolving synaptic pathology in the model.

edges/8.description: Abnormal synaptic architecture is the proposed substrate for network hyperexcitability.

edges/9.description: Network hyperexcitability manifests clinically as the seizure disorder.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype correlation confirms a consistently severe phenotype in p.Arg87 patients but a more variable phenotype in p.Asp724 and other substitutions
evidence.explanation: States the hotspot-dependent severity difference that makes the genotype prognostically informative: Arg87 consistently severe, Asp724 variable.

evidence.snippet: We here report 12 independent patients harboring a variety of de novo variants in CYFIP2 broadening the molecular and clinical spectrum of a novel CYFIP2-related neurodevelopmental disorder
evidence.explanation: Establishes the breadth of the variant spectrum beyond the original hotspot.

evidence.snippet: By structural modeling and investigation of WAVE-regulatory complex (WRC)-mediated actin polymerization in six patient fibroblast lines we assessed the impact of CYFIP2 variants on the WRC
evidence.explanation: Records that the functional assessment was done in six primary patient fibroblast lines, which is what moves the actin finding out of heterologous overexpression.

evidence.snippet: The Arg87Cys variant was present in 12/42 (29%) patients
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the share of cases attributable to the single most common variant, which is what makes Arg87 a hotspot rather than merely a recurrent observation.

genes/0.notes: An in-frame deletion that removes codon 87 entirely, c.258_266del p.(Trp86_Ser88del), has been reported and produces the severe Arg87-hotspot phenotype - consistent with the interface account, since deleting the residue and substituting it have the same structural consequence. Rare truncating variants are reported with a milder phenotype and are of less certain significance; whether they act by haploinsufficiency is not settled, and this entry does not model them as a separate mechanism. The paralog CYFIP1 sits at the same cytogenetic band and lies within the 15q11.2 microdeletion region, but causes a different disorder and is not to be conflated with CYFIP2.

evidence.snippet: When he started having infantile spasms, and there was evidence of small fragments of disorganized activity on EEG, vigabatrin was also started with transitory clinical improvement
evidence.explanation: Records vigabatrin producing only transitory improvement. Marked PARTIAL because it documents an attempted treatment and its limited effect, not an effective one.

treatments/0.description: Seizures are characteristically drug-resistant and typically require multiple agents. No agent is established as preferred in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that de novo Arg87 variants in CYFIP2 have gain-of-function effects on the WAVE signaling pathway
evidence.explanation: The originating statement of the gain-of-function model.

hypotheses/0.description: Hotspot variants destabilize the CYFIP2-WAVE1 interface, weakening sequestration of the VCA domain and releasing the complex to nucleate actin outside normal RAC1 control. On this account the disorder is a toxic gain of function at the level of actin regulation, which distinguishes it from the many developmental and epileptic encephalopathies that act by haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Beyond identifying a decrease in CYFIP2 protein levels in the Cyfip2+/R87C brains, we demonstrated that the p.Arg87Cys variant enhances ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of CYFIP2
evidence.explanation: The originating statement of the destabilization model, measured in brain tissue of the genotype-matched mouse.

hypotheses/1.description: p.Arg87Cys enhances ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of CYFIP2, lowering steady-state protein levels in the brain. On this account the primary consequence is less CYFIP2, not a constitutively active complex. The two accounts are not trivially compatible: one says the complex is inappropriately switched on, the other that there is less of a required subunit.

open_questions/0.rationale: These are not two descriptions of one finding. The gain-of-function account says the complex is inappropriately active because the mutant subunit sequesters VCA more weakly; the destabilization account says there is measurably less CYFIP2 in the brain because the variant protein is ubiquitinated and degraded. A complex missing a required subunit and a complex that is constitutively switched on are different molecular states with opposite implications for therapy - one argues for inhibiting WAVE signalling, the other for restoring CYFIP2 abundance. Both rest on direct measurement: weaker VCA binding and increased actin accumulation in one case, reduced brain protein levels and demonstrated ubiquitination in the other, the latter in a genotype-matched knock-in rather than an overexpression system. A published exchange on exactly this point exists in the literature. The entry therefore draws both edges from the variant node in parallel, tagged to competing hypothesis groups, rather than placing either upstream of the other. Note also that the two accounts are not strictly exclusive - a destabilized interface could plausibly both loosen VCA binding and expose the protein to degradation - but no source demonstrates that reconciliation, and asserting it here would invent a synthesis rather than curate one.

open_questions/1.rationale: The Cyfip2+/R87C mouse passes through three phases: neonatal spasms, then a seizure-free period, then spontaneous recurrent seizures in adulthood ending in premature death. Human DEE65 is described as having intractable seizures from onset, with no reported latent phase. Two readings are possible and they have opposite consequences. If the interval is a species artefact, then the model's adult seizures are not the same illness as the human one and the intervening period should not be used to time interventions. If instead the human trajectory has an under-recognized quiescent phase - plausible, since these children are heavily medicated and profoundly impaired, which makes a partial seizure remission easy to miss - then the model is revealing something about the human course rather than diverging from it. This is a tractable question because it can be settled from existing patient records rather than new experiments.

open_questions/2.rationale: The molecular and cellular end of this disorder is well characterised, and the clinical end is unambiguous, but the step between them is the weakest link in the chain. Actin dysregulation is measured in fibroblasts and transfected cells; seizures are measured in patients and mice; what is not established is the mechanism that converts abnormal spine actin dynamics into synchronous network discharge. The entry marks both edges across this gap as indirect with unknown intermediates rather than asserting a pathway. This matters practically, because it is the step at which any therapy aimed at the actin machinery would have to act on the seizures.

evidence.snippet: The aim of this study was to investigate the mode of inheritance in three individuals with severe early-onset axonal neuropathy and homozygous or compound heterozygous MFN2 mutations.
evidence.explanation: The three founding patients and the two biallelic configurations.

evidence.snippet: We describe a 49-year-old woman with CMT5 associated with compound heterozygosity for two MFN2 variants, one already reported missense mutation (c.748C>T, p.R250W) and a novel nonsense sequence change (c.1426C>T, p.R476*).
evidence.explanation: The named alleles of the family that dissected the dosage mechanism.

evidence.snippet: A review of the literature reveals that sporadic and familial cases of compound heterozygous or homozygous pathogenic MFN2 variants have been infrequently described, which indicates that MFN2 can also be inherited in a recessive manner.
evidence.explanation: The literature-level statement that biallelic MFN2 disease exists and is rare, from the case report that reviewed it.

steps/1.description: Two damaged copies of MFN2, either homozygous or compound heterozygous. Reported configurations span the range: homozygosity for a missense allele in a consanguineous family, homozygosity for a novel allele in a sporadic child, compound heterozygosity for a deletion and a missense allele, and compound heterozygosity for a semidominant missense allele (p.R250W) with a nonsense allele (p.R476*). The last of these is the informative one, because the two alleles are known to behave differently on their own.

evidence.snippet: The p.R250W variant behaves as semidominant by causing only a mild, almost subclinical, neuropathy when heterozygous; the nonsense mutation in the father was phenotypically silent, suggesting that haploinsufficiency for MFN2 is not disease causative, but was deleterious in the daughter who had only one active mutated MFN2 allele.
evidence.explanation: All three dosage states in one family, and the explicit conclusion that haploinsufficiency is not the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Several pathogenic mutations are reported, mainly acting in a dominant fashion, although few sequence variants behaved as recessive or semidominant in rare homozygous or compound heterozygous patients.
evidence.explanation: That MFN2 alleles differ in their dominance behaviour, which is what makes a dosage model necessary rather than a simple dominant/recessive dichotomy.

evidence.snippet: All parents were asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic with some signs of peripheral neuropathy indicating a minimal phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Independent support from a different series: single-allele carriers sit between normal and affected rather than at either end.

steps/2.description:
This node is the entity's defining mechanistic claim and the reason it is a separate disease from its dominant sibling rather than simply a severe version of it. The determinant of disease is the proportion of mitofusin-2 in the cell that is dysfunctional, not the number of mutated alleles.
The evidence for that is a natural experiment. A nonsense allele carried alone is phenotypically silent - no clinical and no electrophysiological neuropathy - so removing half the protein does nothing. A semidominant missense allele carried alone produces a mild, almost subclinical neuropathy, because roughly half the protein is dysfunctional and half is normal. The same missense allele in trans with the nonsense allele produces severe disease, because now essentially all the mitofusin-2 the cell makes is the dysfunctional kind. And two dysfunctional alleles - the homozygous and compound-heterozygous missense patients - give the severe early-onset picture.
The threshold framing is a synthesis of those observations rather than a measured quantity; no study has titrated mutant against wild-type mitofusin-2 in patient neurons.

evidence.snippet: MFN2 is a transmembrane GTPase located on the mitochondrial outer membrane that contributes to mitochondrial fusion, shaping large mitochondrial networks within cells.
evidence.explanation: The protein's molecular identity, location and function.

evidence.snippet: In silico modelling showed that the loss of the TM1 domain resulted in a drastically altered topological insertion of the protein in the mitochondrial outer membrane.
evidence.explanation: How one biallelic allele breaks the protein - a topology change rather than a catalytic one. Graded COMPUTATIONAL because the claim is a modelling result.

evidence.snippet: During the intervening period much has been learned about MFN2 functioning in mitochondrial fusion, calcium signaling, and quality control, and the consequences of these MFN2 activities on cell metabolism, fitness, and development.
evidence.explanation: That fusion is one of several MFN2 activities, which is why this node names fusion specifically rather than treating it as the whole of the protein's function. Graded OTHER because a review's framing is an expert synthesis rather than a study.

steps/3.description: Mitofusin-2 is a transmembrane GTPase of the mitochondrial outer membrane whose job is to tether and fuse adjacent mitochondria, and so to shape the large connected networks that mitochondria form inside cells. Dysfunctional mitofusin-2 breaks that step. One reported homozygous allele shows how directly: an in-frame deletion removing the proline-rich domain and the first transmembrane domain was predicted by modelling to insert into the outer membrane in a drastically altered topology, and the corresponding fibroblasts contained mitochondria tethered to one another but unable to complete fusion.

evidence.snippet: Fetus fibroblasts, investigated by fluorescent cell imaging, electron microscopy and time-lapse recording, showed a sharp alteration of the mitochondrial network, with clumped mitochondria and clusters of tethered mitochondria unable to fuse.
evidence.explanation: The cellular phenotype, with the three methods that established it and the tethered-but-not fused detail.

steps/4.description: Without fusion the network disintegrates. In fibroblasts from a fetus homozygous for an MFN2 deletion, three independent methods - fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and time-lapse recording - showed a sharply altered network with clumped mitochondria and clusters that were tethered to one another but could not fuse. That last detail is mechanistically specific: the tethering step is preserved and the fusion step is not, which localises the defect within mitofusin-2's own reaction rather than to a failure of mitochondria to meet.

evidence.snippet: Multiple deficiencies of respiratory chain complexes with severe impairment of complex I were also evidenced in patient fibroblasts, without involvement of mitochondrial DNA instability.
evidence.explanation: The bioenergetic consequence and the explicit negative finding about mtDNA, which is what rules out the genome-instability route.

steps/5.description:
Fibroblasts from the homozygous fetus showed deficiencies of multiple respiratory chain complexes with complex I most severely affected - and, importantly, without mitochondrial DNA instability. The absence of an mtDNA lesion matters, because MFN2 sits in a group of genes (with OPA1 and POLG) where mtDNA depletion or deletion is a common downstream mechanism; here the bioenergetic defect follows from the disordered network directly rather than through genome damage.
This is a single fibroblast study in the most severe reported genotype, so it is curated as a cellular observation rather than as an established feature of the entity.

evidence.snippet: Here, a different perspective of why, in humans, MFN2 dysfunction preferentially impacts peripheral nerves is provided based on recent insights into its role in determining whether individual mitochondria will be fusion-competent and retained within the cell, or are fusion-impaired, sequestered, and eliminated by mitophagy.
evidence.explanation: The quality-control mechanism this node names, and the reason it is proposed as the link to peripheral nerve. Graded OTHER because a review's proposal is an expert synthesis.

steps/6.description: Fusion competence is how a cell decides which mitochondria to keep: organelles that can fuse are retained in the network, and those that cannot are sequestered and cleared by mitophagy. Losing mitofusin-2 therefore does more than fragment the network - it disrupts that sorting step. A 2020 review proposes this as the reason MFN2 dysfunction preferentially affects peripheral nerve.

evidence.snippet: Evidence for and against a regulatory role of mitofusins in mitochondrial transport is reviewed, nagging questions defined, and implications on mitochondrial fusion, quality control, and neuronal degeneration discussed.
evidence.explanation: The explicit statement that the transport role is contested. INDIRECT because it establishes that the question is open rather than that the mechanism operates, and it is why this node's GO annotation and its edges carry a hedge.

steps/7.description: Reduced delivery of mitochondria along axons to the distal terminals that depend on them. This node is deliberately hedged and kept separate from quality control because its evidence is weaker: the same 2020 review examines the evidence for and against a regulatory role of mitofusins in mitochondrial transport and treats it as an open question, and states that the central mechanism linking mitochondrial abnormalities to dying-back of peripheral nerves is largely unmet. It names a candidate step and does not claim it is proven.

evidence.snippet: Severe early-onset axonal neuropathy (SEOAN) is a heterogeneous phenotype first delineated by Ouvrier et al., characterized by progressive axonal degeneration with gait problems often progressing to wheelchair requirement and later respiratory involvement.
evidence.explanation: The clinical syndrome and its trajectory - axonal degeneration, then gait failure, then respiratory involvement - which is the sequence the phenotypes below follow.

evidence.snippet: the challenge of defining the central underlying mechanism(s) linking mitochondrial abnormalities to progressive dying-back of peripheral arm and leg nerves in CMT2A is largely unmet
evidence.explanation: The dying-back pattern, together with the explicit statement that its mechanism is unsolved. Graded OTHER because a review's assessment is an expert synthesis rather than a study.

steps/8.description:
The clinical disease is a progressive dying-back degeneration of the longest peripheral motor and sensory axons - the arm and leg nerves - producing distal weakness and sensory loss that ascends over time. In the biallelic form the process starts in infancy or early childhood rather than in the second or third decade, progresses to gait failure and often to wheelchair dependence, and reaches respiratory muscle later.
Why peripheral nerve is the tissue that fails is the standing unanswered question of MFN2 biology, and this entry does not answer it. A 2020 review states directly that the challenge of defining the central mechanism linking mitochondrial abnormalities to progressive dying-back of peripheral arm and leg nerves is largely unmet.

evidence.snippet: The aim of this study was to investigate the mode of inheritance in three individuals with severe early-onset axonal neuropathy and homozygous or compound heterozygous MFN2 mutations.
evidence.explanation: The neuropathy and its severity in the three founding patients.

evidence.snippet: We report on a 7-month-old white female with hypotonia, motor delay, distal weakness, and motor/sensory axonal neuropathy in which next-generation sequencing analysis identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants (c.2054_2069_1170del and c.392A>G) in MFN2.
evidence.explanation: The neuropathy characterised as motor and sensory, with the patient's age and genotype.

evidence.snippet: We describe a child carrying a novel homozygous MFN2 mutation leading to an early-onset sensorimotor axonal neuropathy with an atypical and severe phenotype.
evidence.explanation: An independent homozygous patient with the same sensorimotor axonal picture.

evidence.snippet: MFN2 hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (MFN2-HMSN) is a classic axonal peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, inherited in either an autosomal dominant (AD) manner (~90%) or an autosomal recessive (AR) manner (~10%).
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews definition of the neuropathy, covering both inheritance forms.

steps/9.description: A sensorimotor axonal neuropathy is the defining feature and is present in every reported patient. In the biallelic form it is severe and early: the founding series describes it as severe early-onset axonal neuropathy, and a seven-month-old with compound heterozygous variants had motor and sensory axonal neuropathy on nerve conduction study.

evidence.snippet: We report on a 7-month-old white female with hypotonia, motor delay, distal weakness, and motor/sensory axonal neuropathy in which next-generation sequencing analysis identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants (c.2054_2069_1170del and c.392A>G) in MFN2.
evidence.explanation: Distal weakness named among the presenting features of the infant case.

steps/10.description: Distal weakness is the motor expression of the length-dependent axonal loss and was present from seven months of age in the youngest reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Severe early-onset axonal neuropathy (SEOAN) is a heterogeneous phenotype first delineated by Ouvrier et al., characterized by progressive axonal degeneration with gait problems often progressing to wheelchair requirement and later respiratory involvement.
evidence.explanation: Gait problems as a defining component of the syndrome.

steps/11.description: Gait problems are the usual presenting complaint of severe early-onset axonal neuropathy and are the feature that typically brings a child to attention before the diagnosis is made.

evidence.snippet: Severe early-onset axonal neuropathy (SEOAN) is a heterogeneous phenotype first delineated by Ouvrier et al., characterized by progressive axonal degeneration with gait problems often progressing to wheelchair requirement and later respiratory involvement.
evidence.explanation: The wheelchair progression and its qualifier - "often" - which is what sets the frequency band.

steps/12.description: Progression to wheelchair dependence, which is what distinguishes the biallelic form from the typical dominant CMT2A course in which most patients remain ambulant into adult life.

evidence.snippet: Severe early-onset axonal neuropathy (SEOAN) is a heterogeneous phenotype first delineated by Ouvrier et al., characterized by progressive axonal degeneration with gait problems often progressing to wheelchair requirement and later respiratory involvement.
evidence.explanation: Respiratory involvement as a component of the syndrome, and its usual late timing.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights several clinical findings not typically associated with MFN2 pathogenic variants, including young age of onset and rapidly progressing diaphragmatic paresis that necessitated tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation, and adds to the growing list of features identified in autosomal recessive MFN2-related CMT2.
evidence.explanation: The severe respiratory outcome in the infant case, and that it was atypically early.

steps/13.description: Respiratory involvement is a later feature of the syndrome, and in at least one patient it was neither late nor gradual: a seven-month-old with rapidly progressing diaphragmatic paresis required tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights several clinical findings not typically associated with MFN2 pathogenic variants, including young age of onset and rapidly progressing diaphragmatic paresis that necessitated tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation, and adds to the growing list of features identified in autosomal recessive MFN2-related CMT2.
evidence.explanation: The diaphragmatic paresis, its severity, and the authors' framing of it as a feature of the recessive form.

steps/14.description: Rapidly progressive diaphragmatic paresis requiring tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation in a seven-month-old compound heterozygote. The reporting authors present it as a finding not typically associated with MFN2 variants and as an addition to the phenotype of the recessive form specifically.

evidence.snippet: We report on a 7-month-old white female with hypotonia, motor delay, distal weakness, and motor/sensory axonal neuropathy in which next-generation sequencing analysis identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants (c.2054_2069_1170del and c.392A>G) in MFN2.
evidence.explanation: Hypotonia among the presenting features of the infant case.

steps/15.description: Hypotonia at seven months in the youngest reported patient - the infantile presentation of a neuropathy severe enough to be apparent before a child would normally walk.

evidence.snippet: We report on a 7-month-old white female with hypotonia, motor delay, distal weakness, and motor/sensory axonal neuropathy in which next-generation sequencing analysis identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants (c.2054_2069_1170del and c.392A>G) in MFN2.
evidence.explanation: Motor delay among the presenting features of the infant case.

steps/16.description: Motor developmental delay in the infant case, the developmental expression of a neuropathy present before motor milestones are acquired.

evidence.snippet: The prevalence of optic atrophy is approximately 7% in the AD form and approximately 20% in the AR form.
evidence.explanation: The AR-specific figure, approximately 20 percent, which sets the frequency band, and the contrast with the dominant form.

steps/17.description: Optic atrophy, about three times as common in the biallelic form as in the dominant one according to GeneReviews. It is managed with low vision aids and low vision clinic follow-up.

evidence.snippet: MFN2-HMSN is characterized by more severe involvement of the lower extremities than the upper extremities, distal upper-extremity involvement as the neuropathy progresses, more prominent motor deficits than sensory deficits, and normal (>42 m/s) or only slightly decreased nerve conduction velocities (NCVs). Postural tremor is common.
evidence.explanation: Postural tremor stated as common across MFN2-HMSN.

steps/18.description: Postural tremor, which GeneReviews calls common in MFN2 hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic treatment relies on special shoes and/or ankle/foot orthoses to correct foot drop and aid walking; surgery as needed for severe pes cavus; forearm crutches, canes, wheelchairs as needed for mobility; exercise as tolerated; acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents for musculoskeletal pain; treatment of neuropathic pain with tricyclic antidepressants or drugs such as carbamazepine or gabapentin.
evidence.explanation: Pes cavus named as a manifestation that may need surgery in MFN2-HMSN. INDIRECT because it comes from the management section, across both inheritance forms, rather than from a description of biallelic patients.

steps/19.description: High-arched foot deformity, severe enough in some MFN2 patients to be treated surgically.

edges/6.description: Retinal ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve and share the long-axon dependence on mitochondrial fusion; how fusion failure reaches them is not described in the cited sources.

edges/8.description: Whether mitofusin-2 regulates mitochondrial transport is contested, so this edge is a candidate step rather than an established one.

edges/21.description: Postural tremor accompanies MFN2 neuropathy, but no cited source says how the axonal loss produces it.

edges/22.description: Long-standing distal denervation of the foot muscles produces the high-arched foot deformity.

evidence.snippet: A causal relationship between Mitofusin (MFN) 2 gene mutations and the hereditary axonal neuropathy Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) was described over 15 years ago.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease relationship for MFN2 and axonal CMT, long established. Graded OTHER because a review's framing is an expert synthesis rather than a study.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in the MFN2 gene are commonly associated with autosomal dominant (CMT2A2A) or recessive (CMT2A2B) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, with possible involvement of the CNS.
evidence.explanation: The dominant/recessive split named with both designations, which is the clearest published statement that CMT2A2A and CMT2A2B are the two allelic forms of one gene.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in the mitofusin 2 gene (MFN2) are the most common cause of autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT2) disease, which is typically characterized by axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The scale of the dominant disease against which this biallelic form is rare, and the reason the gene's literature is dominated by CMT2A2A.

genes/0.notes:
MFN2 encodes mitofusin-2, an outer-mitochondrial-membrane GTPase. It is the commonest cause of axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and the overwhelming majority of that is the dominant CMT2A2A (OMIM 609260, MONDO:0012231). This entity is OMIM 617087, the biallelic form.
Expert classification. ClinGen's Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel classifies the MFN2 gene-disease relationship for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A2 as Definitive with a **semidominant** mode of inheritance - not autosomal dominant and not autosomal recessive. That single field is the most compact statement of this entity's mechanism available anywhere. It is not cited as an evidence item here: the current assertion is absent from the ClinGen gene-validity snapshot pinned in `data/clingen/MANIFEST.yaml` (`just clingen-refresh` fails on checksum drift), and the older assertion that is in the pin carries a disease label MONDO has since obsoleted. Building a cache file from an unpinned download would commit an artifact that cannot be reproduced from the pin, and repinning is a separate change from curating a disease. The claim was read directly from the ClinGen gene-validity download and is corroborated by the two primary papers cited in the inheritance block, which reach the same conclusion from patient data.
Three traps for anyone extending this entry from the gene rather than from the disease.
First and most important, **biallelic MFN2 does not mean this disease**. Recessive MFN2 variants also cause a lipodystrophy/multiple-symmetric-lipomatosis phenotype that has nothing to do with neuropathy, and MFN2 appears as a rare cause in genetically confirmed familial partial lipodystrophy cohorts; dismech curates that association in `Familial_Partial_Lipodystrophy`.
